passage:
The bell would ring in two minutes, and Zainab dug through her bag for her homework. Out slid her pencil box, tucked under a book. Only yesterday she had shouted at Nazia, "You stole my box!" in front of everyone. Her stomach dropped.
Nazia was already packing her own bag, not looking up. Zainab's face burned; she wanted to pretend nothing had happened. But she walked over.
"Nazia, I was wrong. It was in my bag. I'm sorry I shouted."
Nazia paused, then shrugged. "It's okay. You can borrow my sharpener."
Zainab let out a breath, and when the bell rang they walked out together.

qa.q: Where was Zainab's pencil box?
qa.a: Tucked under a book in her bag.

qa.q: What is Zainab feeling as she finds the pencil box?
qa.a: Guilty and embarrassed. Her stomach drops and her face burns, and she wants to pretend nothing happened.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make in the two minutes before the bell?
qa.a: She walked over to Nazia, said she was wrong, apologised for shouting and told her where the box was.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt during Zainab's apology?
qa.a: Probably relieved and forgiving, since she shrugs and offers to lend a sharpener.

grounding: A child admits an error to a friend and finds the friendship survives.

passage:
Suraj was sure he was right. In the science club he had told everyone that Bhavna's plant-growth table was wrong, and Bhavna had gone quiet. At home he re-measured the seedlings and found that his own ruler had started at the wrong end. His neck went hot. He thought about saying nothing.
The next morning in the school garden he found Bhavna. "I was wrong about your table. My ruler was upside down. Sorry I said it in front of everyone."
Bhavna blinked, then grinned. "I wondered if you'd notice. Help me redo the graph?"
They knelt over the pots together, and Suraj felt lighter than he had all week.

qa.q: What was wrong with Suraj's ruler?
qa.a: It had started at the wrong end.

qa.q: What is Suraj feeling when he finds his own mistake?
qa.a: Ashamed and uncomfortable, since his neck goes hot and he thinks about saying nothing.

qa.q: What choice did Suraj make the next morning?
qa.a: He found Bhavna in the garden, said he was wrong, explained the ruler and apologised for saying it in front of everyone.

qa.q: How does Bhavna seem to feel when Suraj admits it?
qa.a: Relieved and friendly. Bhavna blinks, grins and invites Suraj to redo the graph together.

grounding: A child admits an error to a friend and finds the friendship survives.

passage:
Joseph, you won't say sorry to Samuel? Let me tell you about me and my friend Anand. When I was eleven, I told the whole class that Anand had broken the class clock. I was sure; I'd seen him near it. Anand cried and said it wasn't him.
Two days later the peon told us the clock had fallen on its own when the nail came loose. My stomach dropped. For a whole day I avoided Anand. I was sure he'd never talk to me again if I admitted it.
The next morning I walked up to him at the gate. "I was wrong. I'm sorry I blamed you." My face was burning.
Anand looked at me for a long moment. Then he said, "Okay. Want to share my guavas?" We stayed friends for sixty years. Your Rafiq Dada learned that day that being wrong doesn't end the world.

qa.q: What had actually made the clock fall?
qa.a: The nail came loose and it fell on its own.

qa.q: Why did young Rafiq avoid Anand for a day?
qa.a: Rafiq felt ashamed and afraid that Anand would never talk to him again once he admitted it.

qa.q: Which choice in the story saved the friendship?
qa.a: Walking up to Anand at the gate and saying plainly, "I was wrong. I'm sorry I blamed you."

qa.q: How did Anand respond to the apology?
qa.a: Anand looked at him for a long moment, then offered to share his guavas, and they stayed friends for sixty years.

grounding: Shows a child admitting he was wrong to a friend and discovering the friendship survives.

passage:
Parveen and Yash were building their solar system model at Yash's house the night before it was due, and the power had just gone off. By candlelight they argued over the moon's label.
"The moon makes its own light," Parveen insisted. "Write 'glows'."
"It reflects the sun," said Yash.
"No! I'm sure." They glared at each other. Yash went quiet and hurt.
When the power came back, Parveen checked the science book. Page 42: the moon reflects the sun's light. Parveen's stomach sank. It would be so easy to just change the label and say nothing.
Instead: "Yash... you were right. I was wrong. Sorry I shouted."
Yash shrugged, then grinned. "You can do Saturn's rings, then." They finished at eleven, still friends.

qa.q: Which page of the science book did Parveen check?
qa.a: Page 42.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling on reading page 42?
qa.a: Parveen felt a sinking embarrassment, and was tempted to change the label quietly.

qa.q: What did Parveen choose instead of quietly changing the label?
qa.a: Parveen said plainly, "You were right. I was wrong. Sorry I shouted."

qa.q: How did Yash respond to Parveen's admission?
qa.a: Yash shrugged, grinned and handed over Saturn's rings, and they stayed friends.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a mistake to a friend under deadline pressure and finding the friendship survives.

passage:
In their Chennai apartment block, Keerthana was sure Himani had told everyone about her crush. Who else knew? At evening play time Keerthana wouldn't talk to her and said loudly to the others, "Some people can't keep secrets."
Himani went home early, crying.
That night Keerthana's cousin admitted she had read Keerthana's diary and told her own friend. Keerthana's face went hot. She had been completely wrong about Himani.
The next evening she knocked on Himani's door, heart thumping. "I was wrong. It wasn't you. I'm really sorry I said that in front of everyone."
Himani stood in the doorway, arms crossed. Then she uncrossed them. "You were so mean." "I know." "Okay. Come and see my new puppy."

qa.q: Who had actually told the secret?
qa.a: Keerthana's cousin, who had read the diary.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel on finding out the truth?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and guilty, face hot, realising she had been completely wrong.

qa.q: What made Keerthana's apology work?
qa.a: She went to Himani's door herself, admitted she was wrong, and named the hurt of saying it in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Himani feel before forgiving Keerthana?
qa.a: Himani was hurt and still upset, arms crossed, saying "You were so mean" before softening.

grounding: Shows a child admitting she was wrong to a friend and finding the friendship survives it.

passage:
"Avni, wait." Payal caught up with her at the water cooler. "It's about the science model."
"What about it?"
"I told Ma'am you broke the volcano. I thought you did, because you were holding it."
"I told you, the base was already cracked."
"I know. Rehan said he dropped it before lunch. I was wrong." Payal stared at her shoes. "Sorry. I said it in front of everyone."
Avni was quiet for a moment. "You made me look like a liar."
"I'll tell Ma'am too. Today, before the last bell."
"...Okay." Avni picked at her bottle cap. "Will you help me glue the base after school?"
"Yes. I'll bring the strong glue from home."
Avni bumped her shoulder. "You still owe me for this."

qa.q: Who said he dropped the volcano before lunch?
qa.a: Rehan said he dropped it before lunch.

qa.q: Why did Payal stare at her shoes while she apologised?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of blaming Avni in front of everyone and nervous about how Avni would react.

qa.q: What made Payal's apology work?
qa.a: She named exactly what she got wrong, admitted she said it in front of everyone, and offered to tell Ma'am the same day, so Avni could believe her 🙂

qa.q: How does Avni see the apology?
qa.a: Avni still feels hurt about looking like a liar, but asking for help with the glue and bumping Payal's shoulder show she wants to stay friends.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a mistaken accusation to a friend and discovering that the friendship survives being wrong.
